management.organic_summary: Organic soil amendments, foliar sprays, and pH adjustments are key. Unlock complete guide.
management.chemical_summary: Targeted chemical fertilizers and foliar sprays for specific deficiencies. Upgrade for dosage details.
organic_practices: Conduct a soil test to identify specific nutrient imbalances. Amend soil with well-rotted compost or farmyard manure to improve overall fertility and structure.
Apply foliar sprays of diluted liquid seaweed extract or compost tea to provide readily available micronutrients and stimulate plant health.
For iron deficiency in high pH soils, consider adding elemental sulfur or acidic organic matter to lower soil pH gradually. Incorporate bone meal for phosphorus and potassium source.
chemical_practices: Based on soil test results, apply specific chemical fertilizers. For Nitrogen deficiency, use urea or ammonium sulfate.
For Iron deficiency, apply ferrous sulfate or chelated iron foliar sprays or soil drenches. For Magnesium deficiency, use Magnesium Sulfate (Epsom salts).
Ensure proper soil drainage and aeration to facilitate root health and nutrient uptake, which may involve incorporating gypsum in compacted soils.

disease_info.cause: Nutrient deficiency occurs when the soil lacks essential macro or micronutrients (e.g., Nitrogen, Iron, Magnesium) required for healthy plant growth, or when environmental factors (like unsuitable soil pH, poor drainage, or root damage) prevent the plant from absorbing available nutrients effectively. This leads to impaired chlorophyll production and yellowing of leaves.
disease_info.symptoms: The primary symptom is generalized yellowing (chlorosis) of the leaves. Depending on the specific nutrient, this yellowing might start on older leaves (e.g., Nitrogen, Magnesium) or newer leaves (e.g., Iron), or be interveinal. The plant may also exhibit stunted growth and reduced vigor.
disease_info.cause_summary: Nutrient deficiency results from soil nutrient shortage or absorption issues. Upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Nutrient deficiencies are physiological disorders and do not spread from one plant to another like infectious diseases. Each plant's condition is a direct result of its individual growing environment and nutrient availability.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Generalized leaf yellowing, stunted growth, reduced plant vigor — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Physiological disorder; does not spread between plants. Unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Soil Test & Initial Nutrient Boost
steps.description: Collect soil samples for laboratory testing to precisely identify nutrient deficiencies and pH. Immediately apply 1 kg well-rotted compost per square meter around affected plants to provide a general nutrient boost.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Foliar Feed Application (If General)
steps.description: Prepare a foliar spray with a balanced liquid fertilizer (e.g., NPK 19:19:19 at 5g/liter) or chelated micronutrient mix. Spray leaves thoroughly during early morning to maximize absorption.

steps.label: Day 7 — Observe & Adjust
steps.title: Monitor Plant Response & Water
steps.description: Observe new growth for signs of recovery. Ensure consistent, adequate watering without waterlogging. Adjust irrigation frequency based on soil moisture levels. If soil test results are back, plan targeted application.

steps.label: Day 10 — Targeted Nutrient Input
steps.title: Apply Specific Fertilizer (Post-Test)
steps.description: Based on soil test results, apply the recommended specific fertilizer (e.g., ferrous sulfate for iron, magnesium sulfate for magnesium, or urea for nitrogen) to the soil around plants according to package directions.

steps.label: Day 14 — Review & Ongoing Care
steps.title: Assess Progress & Plan Next Steps
steps.description: Re-evaluate the plant's condition. New leaves should show improved color. Continue with regular monitoring, good watering practices, and appropriate fertilization based on ongoing plant needs and growth stage.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Ginger leaves have a nutrient problem. You can see some leaves turning yellow while others stay green. This condition is called Nutrient Deficiency, often due to lack of minerals like iron, nitrogen, or magnesium. It happens when the soil lacks these nutrients or the plant cannot absorb them properly.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Address nutrient deficiency by soil testing and targeted fertilization promptly for recovery.

Apply Acetamiprid 20% SP at 0.2 grams per liter of water as an alternative vector control rotation.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the Chilli leaf curl virus, which is primarily transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). High temperatures, low humidity, and the presence of infected alternative host weeds or crops in close proximity contribute to the rapid proliferation of the whitefly population, facilitating the spread of the virus to healthy chilli plants.
disease_info.symptoms: Upward curling of leaves, puckering, crinkling, reduction in leaf size, and severe stunting of the plant. Leaves often turn pale green, and infected plants produce fewer flowers and distorted, small chilli fruits.
disease_info.cause_summary: Viral pathogen transmitted by whiteflies — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Mainly spread by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci). It is not transmitted mechanically through touch or tools, nor is it known to be seed-borne in chilli; however, the whiteflies carry the virus from infected weed hosts and adjacent solanaceous crops directly to healthy chilli plants.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Severe upward leaf curling and stunting — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Insect vectors spread the virus quickly — upgrade to learn.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Remove Diseased Plants & Install Traps
steps.description: Uproot and deeply bury severely distorted plants showing advanced curling to prevent the vector from spreading the virus to nearby healthy plants. Install yellow sticky traps near the canopy level.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply First Insecticide Spray
steps.description: Spray systemic Imidacloprid 17.8% SL (0.5 ml/L) thoroughly covering the undersides of the leaves where whiteflies gather and feed.

steps.label: Day 7 — Inspection
steps.title: Monitor Vector Populations
steps.description: Check yellow sticky traps and leaf undersides to evaluate whitefly activity and monitor the progression of healthy new growth.

steps.label: Day 10 — Foliar Spray

steps.description: Spray Acetamiprid 20% SP (0.2 g/L) to prevent whiteflies from developing resistance to the previous chemical application.

steps.label: Day 14 — Final Review
steps.title: Clear Weeds & Soil Check
steps.description: Remove all weeds along field borders to permanently destroy alternative virus hosts and continue monitoring sticky traps.

analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Immediately remove heavily infected plants, set up yellow sticky traps to capture whiteflies, and spray systemic insecticide like Imidacloprid followed by Acetamiprid to suppress the insect vector.

disease_info.cause: Phytophthora Blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora melongenae. This pathogen thrives in warm, wet, and humid conditions with poor air circulation, especially in poorly drained soils. Over-irrigation or heavy rainfall creates ideal conditions for spore germination and infection.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms include irregular, dark brown, water-soaked lesions on leaves, often starting at the leaf margins or tips. These spots rapidly enlarge, turning necrotic and blighted, sometimes with a yellowish halo around the edges. Affected leaves may wither and fall prematurely. Stem lesions can lead to cankers and wilting.
disease_info.cause_summary: Oomycete pathogen thrives in wet conditions, causing rapid tissue decay — upgrade for details.
disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through splashing rain or irrigation water, which carries spores from infected plant debris or soil to healthy plant parts. Wind can also carry spores over short distances. Contaminated soil, infected seeds, and infected seedlings can also introduce the pathogen to new areas. High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness greatly accelerate its spread.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Dark brown, water-soaked leaf spots, leading to blight — unlock full symptom guide.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spreads rapidly via water, wind, and contaminated soil — upgrade for prevention strategies.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Remove infected leaves and apply fungicide
steps.description: Carefully remove all visibly infected leaves and plant debris from the field to reduce inoculum. Apply a contact fungicide like Mancozeb to protect healthy tissues immediately.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Adjust irrigation and improve drainage
steps.description: Switch to drip irrigation if possible, or water at the base of plants in the morning to allow leaves to dry. Ensure proper drainage in beds to avoid waterlogging, which favors pathogen growth.

steps.label: Day 7 — Afternoon
steps.title: Apply systemic fungicide for control
steps.description: Spray a systemic fungicide containing active ingredients like Propamocarb or Dimethomorph. This will help control the existing infection and provide protection to newly growing tissues.

steps.label: Day 10
steps.title: Monitor and continue sanitation
steps.description: Thoroughly inspect plants for new symptoms. If any appear, remove them promptly. Maintain good field hygiene, removing any new fallen leaves or plant debris.

steps.label: Day 14 — Review
steps.title: Evaluate progress and re-apply if needed
steps.description: Assess the disease progression. If symptoms persist or new infections appear, consider another application of a recommended fungicide, potentially alternating active ingredients.

analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Immediately remove infected plant parts. Apply a contact fungicide today, then follow up with a systemic fungicide within a week. Adjust irrigation and improve drainage to prevent further spread.

disease_info.cause: Grey mold is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea, a necrotrophic pathogen that commonly infects carrots post-harvest. It thrives in cool, moist, and humid environments and typically invades through wounds or damaged areas on the carrot roots sustained during harvesting, handling, or transportation. Poor ventilation and condensation within storage facilities also create ideal conditions for its development and spread.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms include soft, watery lesions that develop on the carrot root, often starting at the crown or wounded areas. These lesions rapidly expand and become covered with a dense, fuzzy, grey-brown mold, which is the fungal mycelium and spores. Affected tissues become mushy and rot completely, often leading to significant spoilage of stored carrots.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen thrives in humidity, invading wounds, spreading rapidly — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Grey mold primarily spreads through airborne spores (conidia) released from infected plant material, which can land on and infect wounded or senescent carrot tissues. It also spreads rapidly through direct contact from infected carrots to healthy ones within storage containers. Contaminated harvesting equipment, crates, and storage facilities can also harbor and transmit the fungal spores.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Soft, watery lesions with fuzzy grey mold detected — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Airborne spores infect wounds, spreading via contact and equipment — unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Immediate Action: Isolate and Discard
steps.description: Immediately inspect all harvested carrots. Isolate and discard any carrots showing signs of grey mold or soft rot. Do not compost infected material to prevent further pathogen spread.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Sanitize Storage Environment
steps.description: Thoroughly clean and sanitize all storage bins, crates, and the storage area itself using a strong disinfectant to eliminate any residual fungal spores. Ensure all surfaces are dry before re-stocking.

steps.label: Day 2 — Morning
steps.title: Careful Inspection of Remaining Carrots
steps.description: Re-examine all seemingly healthy carrots for any early, subtle signs of lesions or discoloration that might indicate new infections. Early detection is crucial for minimizing losses.

steps.label: Day 3 — Evening
steps.title: Optimize Storage Conditions
steps.description: Ensure your storage area maintains optimal conditions: cool temperatures (0-4°C) and high humidity (90-95%) with good air circulation. Avoid conditions that lead to condensation on the carrots.

steps.label: Day 4 — Morning
steps.title: Consider Post-Harvest Bio-Fungicide Dip
steps.description: For high-value crops, consider applying an approved post-harvest biological fungicide dip (e.g., based on Bacillus subtilis) to create a protective barrier against further fungal development. Follow product instructions carefully.

steps.label: Day 5 — Afternoon
steps.title: Regular Monitoring of Stored Produce
steps.description: Continue daily or every-other-day monitoring of stored carrots. This vigilance is key to catching new outbreaks quickly and preventing widespread spoilage. Adjust environmental controls as needed.

steps.label: Day 7 — Morning
steps.title: Final Inventory and Storage Reassessment
steps.description: Perform a comprehensive check of all remaining carrots and reassess your storage practices. Identify any recurring issues and plan for improved future harvest and storage management to prevent Grey Mold.

disease_info.cause: Leaf miners are the larvae of certain fly species (Liriomyza spp.) that feed by tunneling through the internal tissue of leaves, creating distinctive winding patterns or 'mines'. Adult female flies lay eggs directly into the leaf tissue. Once hatched, the larvae immediately begin feeding, consuming mesophyll cells and leaving behind air-filled tunnels. The damage disrupts photosynthesis and can weaken the plant.
disease_info.symptoms: Characteristic white or silvery serpentine tunnels are visible on the upper surface of the leaves. These tunnels widen as the larvae grow. Heavy infestations can lead to leaf distortion, premature leaf drop, and reduced plant vigor, impacting overall yield and quality of the fruit.
disease_info.cause_summary: Leaf miner larvae tunnel inside leaves, reducing photosynthesis – upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Leaf miners spread primarily through the flight of adult flies. Female flies lay eggs on the leaves of host plants. After hatching, the larvae remain within the leaf. Upon pupation, they may drop to the soil or remain in the leaf, emerging as new adults to continue the cycle. Rapid reproduction and adult mobility contribute to quick spread within a field and to adjacent crops.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: White serpentine tunnels visible on leaf surface – see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Adult flies rapidly spread eggs to new leaves – unlock complete guide.

disease_info.cause: The fungal pathogen Cercospora moringae is responsible for this disease. disease_info.disease_spread: Cercospora leaf spot spreads primarily through airborne spores, which are readily dispersed by wind and splashing rain from infected plant debris or other diseased plants. Infections can occur pre-harvest and develop rapidly post-harvest, especially during storage.

disease_info.cause: Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (TLCV) is caused by a group of single-stranded DNA viruses from the genus Begomovirus. These viruses are transmitted exclusively by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) in a persistent circulative manner. The virus replicates within the plant cells, disrupting normal cell division and growth, leading to characteristic leaf curling and stunting. High temperatures and high whitefly populations favor disease development and spread.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms include severe upward curling and crinkling of leaves, reduction in leaf size, stunted plant growth, and a bushy appearance. Younger leaves are often more severely affected. Flowers may drop prematurely, and fruit setting is significantly reduced or prevented entirely.
disease_info.cause_summary: Viral pathogen transmitted by whiteflies thrives in warm conditions — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The primary mode of spread is through its insect vector, the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Whiteflies acquire the virus from infected plants and transmit it to healthy ones during feeding. The virus is not typically seed-borne or soil-borne. Wind can aid in the dispersal of whiteflies, thereby facilitating the spread of the disease over wider areas.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Leaf curling, stunted growth, reduced leaf size detected — see full details.

organic_practices: Ensure proper soil drainage and aeration by using a well-draining potting mix or amending field soil with organic matter.
Utilize sterilized potting mix or soil to minimize the presence of pathogens before planting.
Avoid overwatering and ensure irrigation is done early in the day to allow surface moisture to dry.
Apply bio-fungicides containing beneficial microbes like Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens as a soil drench or seed treatment.
Maintain adequate plant spacing to improve air circulation and reduce humidity around seedlings.

disease_info.cause: Damping-off is primarily caused by soil-borne fungal pathogens such as Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium spp., or Fusarium spp. These pathogens thrive in conditions of excessive soil moisture, poor drainage, high humidity, and cool soil temperatures. They attack the roots and lower stem of young seedlings, leading to rot and collapse.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms include yellowing and browning of the lowest, oldest leaves, followed by necrosis and shriveling. The affected leaf may appear water-soaked initially before turning brown. In later stages, the stem often rots at the soil line, causing the seedling to weaken, fall over, and eventually die.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil-borne fungal pathogen Rhizoctonia solani thrives in moist conditions — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: This disease spreads through infected soil, contaminated nursery tools, irrigation water splash, and infested plant debris. The fungal pathogens can persist in the soil for extended periods, making crop rotation and soil sterilization crucial for prevention.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Basal leaves show yellowing, browning, necrosis, and shriveling — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spreads via infected soil, contaminated tools, and water splash — unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Inspect and Isolate Affected Seedlings
steps.description: Carefully inspect all seedlings to identify any other affected plants. Gently remove and dispose of the most severely infected seedlings to prevent further spread to healthy plants. Wear gloves during this process.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Improve Soil Drainage and Airflow
steps.description: Ensure the planting area has good drainage. If in pots, check for clogged drainage holes. For field plants, gently loosen the topsoil around the base of plants to improve aeration and promote faster drying.

steps.label: Day 2
steps.title: Apply Organic Biocontrol Drench
steps.description: Prepare a solution of bio-fungicide containing Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens. Apply this as a gentle soil drench around the base of all remaining seedlings to suppress pathogen growth.

steps.label: Day 4
steps.title: Monitor Plant Progress Closely
steps.description: Observe the affected plants and surrounding seedlings daily for any new or worsening symptoms. Note changes in leaf color, stem condition, and overall vigor. Take photos for comparison.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Reassess Watering Practices
steps.description: Adjust watering frequency and volume to ensure soil remains moist but not waterlogged. Water only when the top inch of soil feels dry. Water early in the morning to allow foliage to dry before evening.

steps.label: Day 9
steps.title: Consider Chemical Fungicide Application
steps.description: If symptoms persist or worsen despite organic measures, apply a soil drench with a chemical fungicide like Azoxystrobin. Follow label instructions precisely for dilution and application rate.

steps.label: Day 12
steps.title: Maintain Optimal Environmental Conditions
steps.description: Continue to ensure good air circulation, appropriate watering, and moderate temperatures. Avoid sudden environmental changes that can stress young plants and make them more susceptible.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Final Evaluation of Plant Health
steps.description: Conduct a comprehensive review of all seedlings. Assess if the disease spread has halted, if plants are recovering, or if further interventions are necessary. Plan for future preventative measures.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Tobacco leaves have a fungal disease affecting seedlings. You can see the lowest leaf turning yellow, then brown, and shriveling. The fungus causing this problem is often called Rhizoctonia solani, which leads to Damping-off. It spreads through infected soil and thrives in overly wet conditions.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Early detection of Damping-off on tobacco seedlings requires immediate action. Improve drainage, apply bio-fungicides like Trichoderma, and consider chemical drench with Azoxystrobin to save plants.

Choose corn varieties known to be less susceptible to physiological leaf spot, if available.
Practice proper irrigation to ensure consistent soil moisture, avoiding both waterlogging and drought stress.
chemical_practices: No chemical fungicides or bactericides are effective as this is not a pathogen-caused disease. Chemical interventions are not recommended for direct treatment.
If a specific nutrient deficiency (like potassium) is confirmed by soil test, appropriate inorganic fertilizers can be applied as a targeted supplement to correct the imbalance.

disease_info.cause: Physiological Leaf Spot is primarily caused by genetic factors in certain corn hybrids, or environmental stressors such as nutrient imbalances (e.g., potassium deficiency), water stress, sudden temperature changes, or high light intensity. It is not caused by an infectious pathogen like a fungus, bacterium, or virus.
disease_info.symptoms: The symptoms typically manifest as irregular, small to medium-sized white to tan spots or lesions on the leaves. These spots lack distinct borders and do not usually contain fungal structures or show bacterial oozing. In severe cases, these spots may coalesce, leading to larger necrotic areas.
disease_info.cause_summary: Genetic predisposition, environmental factors, nutrient imbalances cause this disorder — unlock more.
disease_info.disease_spread: This is a physiological disorder, not an infectious disease. Therefore, it does not spread from plant to plant through wind, rain, insects, or soil. Its occurrence is localized to individual plants based on their genetic susceptibility and environmental conditions.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Irregular white to tan spots visible on leaves — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: This disorder does not spread between plants — unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Optimize watering for consistent soil moisture
steps.description: Ensure the young corn plants receive consistent and adequate moisture. Avoid overwatering which can lead to root issues, and underwatering which causes drought stress. Check soil moisture daily.

steps.label: Day 7 — Afternoon

steps.description: If not done on Day 1, send a soil sample for laboratory testing. This will provide precise information on nutrient levels (especially potassium) and pH, guiding subsequent nutrient management.

steps.label: Day 10 — Morning
steps.title: Apply balanced fertilizer if soil analysis indicates
steps.description: Based on your soil test results, apply a balanced fertilizer or specific nutrient amendments (e.g., potassium-rich options) as needed. Follow recommended dosage carefully to avoid nutrient burn.

steps.label: Day 14 — Monitoring

steps.description: Continue to observe your corn plants closely for any improvement in leaf spot symptoms or the emergence of new healthy growth. Adjust cultural practices as necessary.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Corn leaves have a physiological disorder. You can see irregular white or tan spots on the leaves. This problem is called Physiological Leaf Spot. It usually occurs due to environmental stress or nutrient issues.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Focus on good soil health, balanced nutrition, and consistent watering to help the corn plant recover from physiological leaf spots and stress.

Introduce or encourage natural predators like parasitic wasps, ladybugs, and birds by planting diverse flora.

Emamectin benzoate (e.g., 5% SG) is highly effective against leaf-eating caterpillars.

disease_info.cause: The damage is caused by the feeding activity of chewing insects such as caterpillars (like the Moringa leaf caterpillar), grasshoppers, or beetles. These pests consume leaf tissue, creating visible holes and irregular edges.
disease_info.symptoms: Visible irregular holes on leaves, ragged or chewed leaf margins, and sometimes skeletonized leaves. Young, tender leaves are often most affected, impacting overall plant vigor.
disease_info.cause_summary: Chewing insects damage leaf tissue, creating holes, leading to plant stress — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Pests spread through the movement of adult insects laying eggs on host plants. Larvae hatch and begin feeding locally. Mobile pests like grasshoppers can move between plants, spreading the infestation.
disease_info.scientific_name: Insecta (Various chewing pests, e.g., Noorda moringae)
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Irregular holes, chewed leaf margins, skeletonization observed on leaves — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Insects lay eggs, larvae feed, mobile pests spread locally — unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Inspect and Manually Remove Pests
steps.description: Thoroughly inspect all leaves and branches. Manually pick off any visible caterpillars or larger chewing insects. Destroy them to prevent further spread.

steps.label: Day 1 (Evening)
steps.title: Apply Organic Neem Oil Spray
steps.description: Mix neem oil (1500-3000 ppm azadirachtin) according to label instructions. Spray generously on all affected leaves, ensuring both upper and lower surfaces are covered.

steps.label: Day 4 — Morning
steps.title: Reapply Organic Treatment or Bt
steps.description: Reapply neem oil if pest activity persists. For caterpillars, consider spraying Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for targeted biological control. Apply early morning for best results.

steps.label: Day 7 — Afternoon
steps.title: Assess Damage and Re-evaluate
steps.description: Inspect the plant again to assess the effectiveness of treatments. Look for new damage or live pests. If infestation is severe and organic methods are insufficient, prepare for chemical intervention.

steps.label: Day 8 — Morning (Optional)
steps.title: Chemical Application (if needed)
steps.description: If organic methods failed, apply a chemical insecticide like Emamectin benzoate or Chlorantraniliprole. Follow all safety precautions and dosage recommendations strictly.

steps.label: Day 14 — Ongoing
steps.title: Monitor and Promote Natural Predators
steps.description: Continue monitoring for new pest activity weekly. Maintain a clean field and encourage beneficial insects like ladybugs and predatory wasps to naturally control pest populations in the long term.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Drumstick leaves have a chewing pest problem. You can see irregular holes and chewed edges on many leaves. The pests are various types of insects, like caterpillars or grasshoppers. These insects feed directly on the leaf tissue, causing the damage.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Implement manual pest removal and apply organic neem oil or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) immediately. For severe infestations, consider chemical insecticides like Chlorantraniliprole or Emamectin benzoate, followed by consistent monitoring.

diagnosis.cause: Insufficient availability of potassium in the soil, root damage limiting nutrient uptake, or an imbalance with other nutrients like excessive calcium or magnesium competing for uptake.
diagnosis.cause_summary: Insufficient potassium uptake due to soil imbalance — upgrade for full solution.
diagnosis.disease_spread: Potassium deficiency is a physiological disorder, not a contagious disease. It does not spread from plant to plant but can affect multiple plants if soil conditions or management practices are uniform across an orchard.
diagnosis.symptoms_summary: Leaves show yellowing, reddish-brown margins, and necrosis — unlock complete analysis.
diagnosis.symptoms_description: Leaves exhibit widespread chlorosis (yellowing), particularly between the veins, often progressing to reddish-brown discoloration and necrosis (browning) along the leaf margins and tips. Affected leaves may appear dull and slightly crinkled. Symptoms typically start on older leaves and progress upwards.
diagnosis.disease_spread_summary: Not contagious; impacts plant's overall health and fruit development — learn more.

management.organic_summary: Soil testing and organic potassium sources improve plant vigor — see guide.
management.chemical_summary: Balanced potassium fertilizers enhance nutrient uptake and yield — explore options.
organic_practices: Conduct a comprehensive soil test to confirm potassium levels and pH. Adjust pH if necessary to optimize nutrient availability.
Apply organic potassium sources such as kelp meal, wood ash (use cautiously to avoid excessive pH changes), or compost. Incorporate into the soil around the root zone.
Ensure proper irrigation to prevent water stress, which can hinder nutrient uptake. Avoid waterlogging and drought cycles.
Consider foliar sprays of dilute liquid kelp or other organic potassium solutions for immediate, temporary relief and quicker uptake by leaves.
chemical_practices: Based on soil test results, apply inorganic potassium fertilizers such as potassium sulfate (K2SO4) or muriate of potash (KCl) to the soil. Dosage should be determined by soil analysis.

Utilize foliar sprays of potassium nitrate (KNO3) or other soluble potassium formulations for rapid absorption by leaves, especially during critical growth stages. Follow manufacturer's recommendations for concentration.
Ensure balanced fertilization with other essential nutrients, as an excess of one nutrient can antagonize the uptake of another. Avoid over-application of calcium or magnesium.
management.consumption_safety: Safe

market_quality.reasoning: Severe nutrient deficiency significantly impairs plant vigor, leading to poor fruit set, reduced fruit size, quality, and overall yield. Fruits from affected plants are often small, lack proper color and flavor, and have poor storage characteristics.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Conduct Soil Test and Prepare Foliar Spray
steps.description: Collect soil samples from different areas of the orchard for a comprehensive nutrient analysis, focusing on potassium. While awaiting results, prepare a foliar spray with a soluble potassium fertilizer (e.g., potassium nitrate at 0.5-1% solution or a liquid kelp product). Apply the spray evenly to the foliage, preferably in the early morning or late afternoon.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Organic/Inorganic Soil Amendments
steps.description: Based on initial assessment and without full soil test results, apply a moderate dose of a slow-release potassium source around the root zone of affected plants. For organic, use well-rotted compost or kelp meal. For chemical, use potassium sulfate. Ensure even distribution and light incorporation into the topsoil, followed by light irrigation.

steps.label: Day 7 — Afternoon
steps.title: Re-evaluate Symptoms and Adjust Irrigation
steps.description: Observe plants for any signs of improvement or worsening symptoms. Take photos to track progress. Check soil moisture levels and adjust irrigation schedule as needed to ensure consistent moisture, avoiding both waterlogging and drought, which can impair nutrient uptake.

steps.label: Day 10 — Morning
steps.title: Second Foliar Application if Symptoms Persist
steps.description: If symptoms of potassium deficiency are still prominent or only show slight improvement, apply a second foliar spray of potassium fertilizer. Use the same concentration as Day 1. If soil test results have arrived, use them to fine-tune the long-term fertilization strategy.

steps.label: Day 14 — Afternoon
steps.title: Monitor Plant Health and Plan Future Steps
steps.description: Continue monitoring the plants regularly for new leaf development and overall vigor. Plan for the full implementation of a balanced fertilization program based on your soil test results. Consistent nutrient management is key for long-term plant health and productivity.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Pomegranate has a nutrient deficiency. You can see leaves turning yellow, then reddish-brown, especially at the edges. The specific problem is Potassium Deficiency. This occurs when the plant does not get enough potassium from the soil.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Quickly address potassium deficiency through soil amendments and foliar feeds for plant recovery.

management.organic_summary: Improve drainage and soil health using organic methods — unlock complete guide.
management.chemical_summary: No direct chemical solution for waterlogging; focus on drainage. Upgrade for complete guide.
organic_practices: Improve soil drainage: Incorporate organic matter like compost or well-rotted manure to improve soil structure, aeration, and drainage.
Raise planting beds: For areas consistently prone to waterlogging, consider planting tomatoes on raised beds to ensure better root aeration and drainage.

Mulching: Apply a layer of organic mulch (e.g., straw, wood chips) around the base of plants (once soil has dried) to help regulate soil moisture, but ensure it doesn't trap excess moisture directly around the stem.
chemical_practices: No direct chemical treatments are available for waterlogging stress, as it is a physical and environmental issue. The primary focus for management is on physical drainage and soil improvement practices.

disease_info.cause: Prolonged saturation of soil with water, leading to a lack of oxygen for roots, impaired respiration, nutrient leaching, and root damage.
disease_info.symptoms: Wilting, yellowing or pale leaves, stunted growth, leaf curling, and overall reduced plant vigor.
disease_info.cause_summary: Excess water deprives roots of oxygen, leading to plant stress. Upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: This is a non-transmissible physiological disorder, not spread by pathogens or vectors. It occurs under specific environmental conditions affecting plants exposed to similar issues.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Wilting, yellowing leaves, stunted growth detected — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Not a spreading disease; affects plants under similar water conditions. Unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Ensure immediate soil drainage or relocate plant
steps.description: Carefully remove the plant from the waterlogged area or create drainage channels to quickly remove standing water around its roots. Prolonged submergence is fatal.

steps.label: Day 2 — Morning
steps.title: Assess root health and gently aerate soil
steps.description: Once water recedes, gently loosen the soil around the plant's base using a hand fork or trowel. This allows air to reach the suffocated roots without causing further damage.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply a diluted organic root stimulant
steps.description: To aid recovery, apply a weak solution of humic acid or seaweed extract to the soil. This encourages the development of new, healthy roots. Avoid overwatering.

steps.label: Day 7 — Morning
steps.title: Monitor plant for signs of recovery or decline
steps.description: Observe the plant closely for new growth, improved leaf color, and reduced wilting. Take photographs to track progress and identify any lingering issues.

steps.label: Day 10 — Morning
steps.title: Apply a balanced, mild liquid fertilizer
steps.description: If the plant shows clear signs of recovery, provide a very light application of a balanced liquid fertilizer (e.g., 5-1-1 NPK) to support new growth. Do not over-fertilize.

steps.label: Day 14 — Morning
steps.title: Maintain consistent, appropriate watering schedule
steps.description: Continue watering only when the top inch of soil is dry. Ensure excellent soil drainage is maintained for future prevention to avoid recurrence of waterlogging.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Tomato leaves have a serious physiological problem. You can see wilting, yellowing leaves, and stunted growth. The plant is suffering from Waterlogging Stress. It occurs when roots are submerged in too much water, suffocating them.

disease_info.cause: Caused by the fungus Pestalotiopsis palmarum, which thrives in warm, humid conditions. It can infect leaves, particularly those stressed by environmental factors or nutrient deficiencies. Spores are easily disseminated by wind and splashing rain.
disease_info.symptoms: Small, circular to irregular yellowish spots appear on the older leaves. These spots gradually turn brownish-gray with darker margins and may sometimes coalesce into larger necrotic areas. Minute black dots (acervuli) might be visible within the spots.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen thrives in humidity, spreading fast — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through airborne spores, which are dispersed by wind and splashing rain. High humidity, prolonged leaf wetness, and dense planting favor spore germination and infection, leading to wider spread within the farm.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Small yellowish-brown spots detected on leaves — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores carried by wind and rain, infecting new leaves — unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Sanitation and Pruning of Infected Leaves
steps.description: Carefully remove any leaves showing significant yellowish-brown spots or lesions. Use clean, sharp pruning tools and dispose of the infected material by burning or burying it away from healthy palms to prevent further spread of spores.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Improve Air Circulation and Drainage
steps.description: Ensure good air circulation around the coconut palms. This may involve weeding around the base of the palms or pruning other non-essential vegetation nearby. Good drainage prevents waterlogging which can stress plants.

steps.label: Day 7 — Afternoon
steps.title: Apply Organic Biofungicide Spray
steps.description: Prepare and apply a biofungicide solution, such as one containing Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis, to the foliage. Follow product instructions for dilution and application rates to protect new and existing leaves.

steps.label: Day 10 — Morning
steps.title: Monitor for New Symptoms and Progress
steps.description: Regularly inspect the leaves, especially newly emerging ones, for any new spots or signs of disease progression. Note down observations to assess the effectiveness of the initial management steps.

steps.label: Day 14 — Afternoon
steps.title: Consider Chemical Application if Symptoms Persist
steps.description: If new symptoms appear or existing ones worsen despite organic treatments, consider a chemical fungicide. Apply a broad-spectrum fungicide like Copper oxychloride, following all safety guidelines and dosage instructions on the label.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Coconut leaves have a fungal leaf spot problem. You can see small, irregular yellowish-brown spots appearing on the leaf surface. The fungus causing this condition is Pestalotiopsis palmarum. It spreads easily through wind and splashing rain.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Early detection allows simple sanitation, cultural practices, and organic sprays to manage this minor fungal leaf spot, preventing further spread effectively.

organic_practices: Remove and destroy infected crop residues after harvest to reduce soil inoculum.
Implement drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for at least three years.
Apply copper-based organic fungicides or bio-agents like Trichoderma viride to suppress fungal development.
chemical_practices: Apply protective fungicides containing Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil early in the disease cycle.
Rotate chemical classes using systemic options like Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole or Boscalid + Pyraclostrobin to prevent resistance development.

disease_info.cause: The fungal pathogen Stemphylium vesicarium attacks onion foliage, particularly when plants are stressed, physically damaged, or subjected to prolonged periods of warm, wet weather.
disease_info.symptoms: Yellowing and browning at the leaf tips, progressing down the leaf blades. Developing tan to light brown, water-soaked lesions that later become dark olive-brown to black as spores form, causing premature leaf dieback.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen attacks stressed onion foliage in warm wet conditions — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread: Spores are spread primarily by wind and splashing water. Overwinters on infected crop debris in the soil, which serves as the primary inoculum for the next crop cycle.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Yellowing leaf tips progressing to dark brown lesions — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores spread by wind and splashing rain — upgrade.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Remove Damaged Foliage and Clean Field
steps.description: Prune and destroy severely yellowed or blighted tips from onions in small plots to reduce the immediate spore load. Ensure field tools are sanitized before and after use.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply First Fungicidal Spray Treatment
steps.description: Apply a preventive fungicide spray like Mancozeb at 2g per liter of water, or an organic copper hydroxide spray, ensuring uniform coverage across the green foliage.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Optimize Irrigation and Soil Nutrition
steps.description: Ensure drip lines are functioning correctly to avoid standing water. Avoid over-applying nitrogen fertilizer, which produces succulent leaf tissue highly susceptible to fungal penetration.

steps.label: Day 10 — Morning
steps.title: Rotate Fungicide Application
steps.description: Apply a systemic fungicide mix such as Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole at recommended label rates (e.g., 1 ml per liter of water) to arrest internal fungal development.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Monitor Field and Re-evaluate Symptoms
steps.description: Inspect new leaf growth for any signs of yellowing or tip-burn. Continue field monitoring weekly and repeat protective sprays if wet weather conditions persist.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Onion has a fungal foliage disease. You can see yellowing and drying of the leaf tips progressing downwards into tan colored lesions. The fungus is called Stemphylium vesicarium. It spreads through windborne spores and thrives when foliage remains wet for extended periods.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: To manage Stemphylium leaf blight, immediately prune affected leaf tips, optimize soil nutrition, ensure dry foliage by utilizing the existing drip irrigation, and apply a rotated sequence of protective (Mancozeb) and systemic (Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole) fungicides.

disease_info.cause: Cottony Leak is caused by the water mold Pythium aphanidermatum. This pathogen thrives in high humidity and warm temperatures, typically infecting cucumber fruits through wounds or natural openings (like the blossom end) during harvesting, packing, or storage. A persistent film of water on the fruit surface and poor ventilation significantly contribute to its rapid development.
disease_info.symptoms: The symptoms begin as soft, watery lesions that quickly expand across the fruit surface. These affected areas become visibly covered with a dense, white, cottony fungal growth, leading to a rapid and complete decay of the entire cucumber fruit. Yellowing and softening precede the visible mold.
disease_info.cause_summary: Oomycete thrives in high humidity, infecting wounds — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Pythium aphanidermatum primarily spreads through contaminated irrigation water, infected soil, or crop debris in the field. Post-harvest, it spreads rapidly from infected fruits to healthy ones through direct contact, especially under wet conditions and poor ventilation during transport and storage.

disease_info.cause: Powdery Mildew on grapes is caused by the fungus Erysiphe necator (also known as Uncinula necator). This pathogen thrives in warm, moderately humid conditions (optimal temperatures around 20-27°C) and unlike many other fungi, does not require free water on the leaf surface for germination or infection. It overwinters as chasmothecia (small, dark fruiting bodies) on the bark of vines or in dormant buds. Spores are released in spring and initiate primary infections.
disease_info.symptoms: The primary symptom is the appearance of white, powdery patches on the surface of leaves, shoots, flowers, and most critically, on the grape berries. Infected berries may become stunted, discolored (often brownish-grey), and can crack, making them susceptible to secondary infections like sour rot. Severely infected young shoots can be distorted and fail to develop properly. A characteristic 'burnt' odor can sometimes be detected in severely infected vineyards.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen thrives in humidity, spreading fast — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Powdery Mildew primarily spreads through wind-borne spores (conidia). These spores can travel long distances and infect new plants. While rain can wash spores, it is not required for spore germination or infection, making it a significant threat even in dry periods with high humidity. Contaminated vineyard equipment, clothing, and even insect activity can contribute to localized spread.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: White powdery patches on berries, discolored and shriveled — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores spread by wind; rain less significant — unlock complete guide.

disease_info.cause: Boron deficiency is a physiological disorder caused by an inadequate supply of boron in the soil, which is essential for cell wall formation, sugar transport, and division in meristematic tissues. Sandy, highly leached, or highly alkaline soils restrict boron availability, leading to hollow stems and brown browning on the curd surface.
disease_info.symptoms: The symptoms appear as light brown, water-soaked, or discolored patches on the head (curd) of the cauliflower. Internally, the stem may develop hollow, dark cavities, and the overall curd may taste bitter and have reduced compactness.

disease_info.disease_spread: This is a physiological disorder, not an infectious disease. It does not spread from plant to plant. However, it can affect the entire field simultaneously if the soil boron levels are universally low or if soil conditions limit boron uptake.

disease_info.cause: White mold is caused by the fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. It thrives in cool, moist conditions with high humidity, particularly when plants are dense or canopy closure occurs. When conditions are favorable, these sclerotia germinate to produce apothecia (small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies) that release airborne ascospores. These ascospores infect senescent plant tissues or wounds, leading to disease development. The disease is often exacerbated by over-irrigation or poor drainage.

Affected tissues become soft, watery, and rot rapidly. As the disease progresses, hard, black, irregularly shaped sclerotia, resembling rat droppings, form within the rotted tissue and on the external mycelial mat. This can lead to complete collapse of the plant.

disease_info.disease_spread: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum primarily spreads through its sclerotia, which can be disseminated by contaminated soil, irrigation water, farm equipment, and infected plant debris. Ascospores, released from apothecia, are wind-dispersed and can infect new plants over short distances. Seed contamination can also introduce the pathogen to new areas.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by Peronosclerospora sorghi, an oomycete pathogen. It is favored by high soil moisture, cool temperatures during seedling emergence, and high relative humidity. Systemic infection occurs when the pathogen infects young corn seedlings via soilborne oospores or windborne conidia.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms include pale yellow to white chlorotic stripes on the leaves, starting from the leaf base and extending upwards. A white, downy fungal growth (conidia and conidiophores) can be observed on the underside of infected leaves under humid conditions. Plants may be stunted, and ears may be partially or completely sterile.

disease_info.disease_spread: Primary infection occurs from soilborne oospores that can survive in the soil for several years. Secondary spread occurs during the growing season via windborne conidia under high humidity and moderate temperatures.

disease_info.cause: Caused by the oomycete Pseudoperonospora cubensis. It thrives in cool, moist conditions with high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness. Spores (sporangia) germinate on wet leaf surfaces.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms are small, angular, yellowish spots on the upper leaf surface, often delimited by veins. These spots enlarge and become necrotic (brown and dead). In severe cases, widespread chlorosis and defoliation occur, leading to reduced fruit quality and yield. Grayish to purplish fungal growth may be visible on the leaf undersides.

disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through wind-borne sporangia (spores) that travel long distances. Rain splash also aids in local dispersal. Infected plant debris, contaminated tools, and, less commonly, seeds can also contribute to spread. Ideal conditions include temperatures between 15-25°C and prolonged leaf wetness.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by Rice grassy stunt virus (RGSV), a member of the genus Tenuivirus. It is transmitted exclusively by the brown planthopper (BPH) vector, Nilaparvata lugens, in a persistent, circulative manner. The virus does not spread mechanically or through seed, meaning infection depends entirely on insect feeding activity on susceptible rice varieties.
disease_info.symptoms: Affected rice plants show severe stunting, an excessive number of erect and narrow tillers, and a grassy, bunchy appearance. Leaves are significantly narrowed, pale green to pale yellow, and often show small brown spots or mottling. Infected plants rarely produce panicles; if any are formed, they are dark, small, and contain empty or unfilled grains.

disease_info.disease_spread: Spread occurs primarily through the brown planthopper (BPH) vector. Once the insect acquires the virus after feeding on infected weeds or volunteer rice plants, it remains infective for life and transmits the virus to healthy plants during feeding. Warm, humid weather that favors BPH population explosions significantly increases disease transmission rates.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Stunted bunchy growth with yellowing leaves - see full details.

diagnosis.cause: The disease is caused by the Papaya ringspot virus (PRSV), a member of the Potyvirus family, which disrupts chlorophyll production and normal plant growth.
diagnosis.cause_summary: Potyvirus infection disrupting chlorophyll and development — upgrade now.
diagnosis.disease_spread: The virus is transmitted in a non-persistent manner by several species of aphids (such as Myzus persicae and Aphis gossypii) during feeding, as well as through infected planting material and mechanical tools.
diagnosis.symptoms_summary: Distorted mosaic leaves showing puckered chlorosis — see full details.
diagnosis.symptoms_description: Leaves display severe mosaic patterns, yellow mottling, chlorosis, and blistering. Newly formed leaves are distorted, puckered, wrinkled, and significantly reduced in size. Dark green streaks may also appear on the petioles and stems.
diagnosis.disease_spread_summary: Aphid vectors transmit viral pathogen during feeding — upgrade today.

management.organic_summary: Rogueing infected hosts and barrier crops prevents spread — upgrade.
management.chemical_summary: Vector control using systemic insecticides manages dissemination — upgrade.
organic_practices: Remove and immediately destroy infected plants to reduce local virus reservoirs.
Intercrop with barrier crops such as maize or sorghum to disrupt aphid flight paths and feeding.
Apply organic neem oil sprays (0.5% to 1%) to repel aphid vectors.
Cover young plants in nurseries with insect-proof netting.
chemical_practices: No chemical curative treatment exists for the viral infection itself.
Apply systemic insecticides such as Imidacloprid or Dimethoate to manage aphid vector populations.
management.consumption_safety: Toxic/Discard

market_quality.reasoning: Severe viral infections distort foliar development, resulting in stunted plant growth, poor fruit set, and ring-spotted, unmarketable papayas with flat taste.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the fungal pathogen Thielaviopsis paradoxa (also known as Ceratocystis paradoxa). It enters the coconut palm stem through growth cracks, mechanical injuries, or wounds caused by pruning and harvesting. Excessive soil moisture, poor drainage, and heavy clay soils, combined with high humidity, create highly favorable conditions for the fungus to establish and colonize the vascular tissues of the trunk.
disease_info.symptoms: The primary symptom is the exudation of a dark reddish-brown to black liquid from cracks on the trunk, which later turns black as it dries. The tissue beneath the bleeding point becomes soft, rotted, and discolored yellow to dark brown. In advanced stages, the leaves turn yellow, droop, and dry up prematurely, starting from the lower whorls. The crown may become smaller, and the overall yield of the palm drops drastically as the internal vascular system gets heavily compromised.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen enters stem wounds under high moisture—upgrade today.
disease_info.disease_spread: The fungus spreads primarily through wind, rain splashes, and irrigation water carrying spores from infected palms or contaminated soil. Mechanical tools used for harvesting or pruning that are not sterilized can easily transmit the pathogen from a diseased tree to a healthy one. The fungus can also survive in the soil or decaying plant debris for extended periods, waiting for a host or entry wound.

disease_info.cause: Phomopsis Blight is caused by the fungus Phomopsis vexans. This pathogen thrives in warm, humid, and wet conditions. Spores are released from infected plant debris or previously infected plants and spread by wind, rain splash, or irrigation water, infecting new plant tissue through natural openings or wounds. Overcrowding and poor air circulation contribute to its development.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms include numerous small, circular to irregular dark brown spots on the leaves, often with a yellowish halo. As lesions enlarge, they may coalesce, becoming darker brown to black. Tiny black dots (pycnidia, which are fungal fruiting bodies) may become visible within the older spots, particularly on the underside of the leaf. Severe infection can lead to leaf blight and defoliation.

disease_info.disease_spread: Phomopsis vexans spreads primarily through wind, rain splash, and irrigation water carrying fungal spores from infected plant debris, soil, or nearby diseased plants. It can also be seed-borne. Contaminated tools and hands can also spread the disease. High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness are critical for spore germination and infection.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the soil-borne fungal pathogen Athelia rolfsii (synonym Sclerotium rolfsii). It thrives in warm, humid weather combined with wet soils. The fungus targets the stem at or near the soil line, blocking the vascular system and preventing water and nutrients from reaching the upper leaves, leading to wilting and decay.
disease_info.symptoms: Yellowing and sudden wilting of branches, brown lesions at the stem base near the soil line, and the presence of white, fan-like fungal thread (mycelium) along with tiny round mustard-seed-like structures (sclerotia) on the infected stem and soil surface.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil fungal pathogen attacks lower stems - unlock full treatment details.
disease_info.disease_spread: The pathogen survives in the soil as sclerotia for many years. It spreads through infected soil movement, contaminated farm equipment, running irrigation water, and infected crop residues left in the field.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Stem browning and localized wilting detected - see diagnosis details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Pathogen spreads easily via soil and water - learn more.

disease_info.cause: Damping-off is primarily caused by soil-borne oomycetes such as Pythium species. It thrives in conditions where there is excessive soil moisture, poor drainage, cool soil temperatures, and overcrowded seedling placement. The pathogen attacks the tender stems and roots of young onion seedlings near the soil line, leading to tissue decay.
disease_info.symptoms: The symptoms are characterized by young onion seedlings collapsing at the soil surface, displaying girdled, water-soaked, and shriveled stems. Roots are often rotted, mushy, and discolored brown or black. Affected patches of seedlings quickly thin out and die in circular patterns within the nursery bed.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil pathogens thrive in wet conditions - upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The pathogen spreads through contaminated soil, splashing water, shared nursery tools, and infected plant debris. Wind and heavy rain can wash the soil-borne spores from diseased patches to healthy areas of the nursery bed, rapidly accelerating the infection.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Seedlings collapse at the soil line - see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Water splashing and wet soil spreads disease - unlock complete guide.

Apply neem oil or Bacillus subtilis-based bio-fungicides to suppress spore germination.
Mulch the base of the plant to prevent soil-borne spores from splashing onto foliage.
chemical_practices: Spray copper-based fungicides such as Copper Oxychloride.
Apply systemic fungicides containing Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, or Azoxystrobin according to label instructions.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria solani, which thrives in warm, humid conditions with frequent rainfall or overhead irrigation. It overwinters in crop debris, wild solanaceous hosts, and contaminated soil.
disease_info.symptoms: Irregular brown spots with concentric rings resembling a target pattern appear on older leaves first. These spots are often surrounded by a yellow chlorotic halo, eventually causing the leaves to dry up, die, and fall off.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen thrives in humidity, spreading fast — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Spores are carried primarily by wind, splashing water from rain or overhead irrigation, contaminated tools, and human contact. The pathogen can also persist in infected seeds and soil.
disease_info.disease_summary: Fungal spores spread via wind and rain splash — unlock complete details.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Concentric rings and yellow margins detected — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores spread by wind and water splashing — unlock complete details.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Pruning and Sanitation
steps.description: Carefully prune away heavily infected lower leaves showing target-like spots and yellow halos. Safely discard or burn the infected plant debris far from the field to reduce spore load.

steps.label: Day 2 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Mulch around Base
steps.description: Spread a clean layer of straw or plastic mulch around the base of the plants. This physical barrier prevents fungal spores residing in the soil from splashing onto the healthy leaves during watering.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: First Fungicide Application
steps.description: Spray a preventative or curative fungicide such as Mancozeb or Copper Oxychloride thoroughly covering both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Apply early in the morning when wind is low.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Adjust Irrigation Method
steps.description: Ensure watering is done strictly at the soil level using drip irrigation or a watering can. Avoid overhead watering to keep leaf surfaces dry, which deprives the fungus of required moisture.

steps.label: Day 10
steps.title: Follow-up Fungicide Spray
steps.description: Perform a second targeted application of fungicide, alternating active ingredients (such as using Azoxystrobin) to prevent the pathogen from developing resistance.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Monitor and Review
steps.description: Inspect new growth for symptoms of dark concentric rings. If the spread has stopped and new leaves look clean and green, maintain weekly scouting and dry cultural practices.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Tomato leaves have a fungal infection. You can see dark brown spots with target-like concentric rings surrounded by yellow margins. The fungus is called Alternaria solani. It spreads through wind, splashing rain, and contaminated soil.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Prune infected lower foliage immediately, apply mulching to prevent splashback, and spray copper-based or systemic fungicides like Mancozeb to halt the fungal spread.

Dust the leaves with diatomaceous earth to repel the pests.
chemical_practices: Spray Cypermethrin 10% EC to control severe infestations.
Apply Spinosad 45% SC targeting the foliage where beetles feed.

disease_info.cause: The damage is caused by small, jumping flea beetles feeding on the leaves, creating characteristic small, round holes.
disease_info.symptoms: Shot-hole appearance on the leaves, with multiple small, circular holes chewed through the leaf blades.
disease_info.cause_summary: Pest feeding causes characteristic tiny leaf holes - unlock full guide.
disease_info.disease_spread: Adult beetles jump from plant to plant and can fly short distances, rapidly spreading across the field.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Numerous small circular shot-holes on leaf surface - upgrade now.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Install Sticky Traps
steps.description: Place yellow sticky traps at canopy level near the affected plants to monitor and catch jumping beetles.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Neem Oil Spray
steps.description: Mix 5ml of neem oil per liter of water with a few drops of liquid soap and spray thoroughly on both sides of the leaves.

steps.label: Day 10 — Follow Up
steps.title: Inspect Leaves for New Holes
steps.description: Check the fresh new growth for any signs of fresh shot-holes; repeat neem spray if active beetles are still present.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Brinjal leaves have a pest infestation problem. You can see small, round shot-holes chewed through the leaf blades. The tiny insect responsible is called the Flea Beetle. It spreads by jumping or flying from plant to plant, especially in warm, dry weather.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Install yellow sticky traps immediately and spray neem oil to repel the active beetles feeding on the leaves.

management.organic_summary: Eradication and crop rotation help reduce bacterial population — unlock complete guide.
management.chemical_summary: Soil drenching with copper and antibiotics limits spread — upgrade for dosage guide.
organic_practices: Uproot and safely destroy infected plants by burning or burying them far from the field.
Incorporate bio-control agents like Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma viride into the surrounding soil.
Implement a strict crop rotation of 3-4 years with non-solanaceous crops such as maize, ragi, or legumes.
Improve soil drainage and raise planting beds to avoid waterlogging.
chemical_practices: Apply copper oxychloride (3g/liter of water) as a soil drench around the root zones of surrounding healthy plants.
Drench the soil with Streptocycline (1g in 10 liters of water) to suppress bacterial activity in early infestation stages.
Disinfect all farming implements and shoes with a chlorine solution before moving to uninfected blocks.
management.consumption_safety: The plant itself is infected and dying; any small developing fruits on this specific wilting plant are of poor quality and should not be harvested for consumption.

disease_info.cause: A soil-borne bacterium that enters through root systems, rapidly multiplying to clog and destroy the vascular water-transporting xylem tissues.
disease_info.symptoms: Rapid, sudden wilting of the lower leaves during the warmer parts of the day, followed by complete plant collapse without initial yellowing. If the stem is cut, the vascular bundles appear dark, and a milky white bacterial ooze can emerge when placed in water.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil-borne bacterial pathogen clogs water-transporting vascular system — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread: Spread primarily through contaminated irrigation water, wet soil movement, infected farm tools, transplanted seedlings, and root-to-root contact.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Sudden foliage wilting and stem vascular browning occurring rapidly — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Bacteria spreads easily via wet soil and shared water — upgrade.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Isolate and Remove Diseased Plants
steps.description: Carefully dig out the wilted brinjal plant along with its immediate root ball and soil. Dispose of it far away from the field to prevent localized pathogen spread.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Targeted Soil Drench
steps.description: Drench the soil of surrounding healthy plants with Streptocycline (0.1 g/liter) and copper oxychloride (3 g/liter) to create a protective barrier.

steps.label: Day 7 — Afternoon
steps.title: Adjust Irrigation and Drainage
steps.description: Ensure no water flows from the infected zone to healthy plots. Reduce irrigation frequency to prevent soggy soil conditions that favor bacterial multiplication.

steps.label: Day 14 (Evaluation)
steps.title: Monitor Field and Apply Bio-agents
steps.description: Scan the plot for any new signs of wilting. Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens formulations near the root zones of remaining plants to boost soil suppression.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Brinjal has a bacterial infection. You can see sudden wilting of the leaves and stems while they still remain green. The pathogen is called Ralstonia solanacearum. It spreads through contaminated soil water, infected agricultural tools, and close root contact between roots.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Immediately pull out and burn the infected plant. Drench the surrounding soil with copper oxychloride or streptocycline to protect healthy neighbors, and strictly avoid water run-off from the infected area.

chemical_practices: Root feed with Hexaconazole or Propiconazole solutions.
Soil drench the basin of infected and neighboring palms with Carbendazim or Copper Oxychloride to prevent pathogen spread.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the soil-borne wood-rotting fungus Ganoderma lucidum, which infects the root system and base of the stem, often triggered by water stagnation, poor drainage, and lack of organic soil fertility.
disease_info.symptoms: The lowest fronds show signs of yellowing, severe wilting, and complete drying, eventually hanging down around the stem. The stem base becomes discolored, and internal tissues rot, severely restricting water and nutrient transport.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil fungal pathogen attacks root systems - upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The fungus spreads primarily through the soil via root-to-root contact, contaminated agricultural implements, and airborne spores released from mature bracket-like fungal structures.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Dry drooping lower fronds indicate root rot - unlock complete details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spreads through soil contact and fungal spores - explore transmission patterns.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Isolate the Infected Palm
steps.description: Dig a trench 30 cm wide and 60 cm deep about 1 meter away from the trunk of the infected palm to physically sever root contacts with healthy neighboring trees.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Bio-control Drenching
steps.description: Prepare a mixture of Trichoderma harzianum with organic compost and enrich the basin of the palm to suppress the pathogenic Ganoderma fungus.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Targeted Fungicide Root Feeding
steps.description: Carefully expose an active root of the palm, cut it at an angle, and insert it into a pouch containing 2 ml of Hexaconazole mixed in 100 ml of water.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Monitor and Improve Drainage
steps.description: Check neighboring palms for early yellowing and ensure there is no water logging in the block, as excess moisture favors fungal multiplication.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Arecanut leaves have a fungal root infection. You can see the lower frond completely drying up and drooping while the upper crown remains green. The soil-borne fungus is called Ganoderma. It spreads through the soil by root contact and thrives in poorly drained conditions.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Dig an isolation trench around the affected tree immediately. Drench the soil with Trichoderma and perform root-feeding using Hexaconazole to stop root-rot advancement.

management.organic_summary: Biological seed treatment controls soil fungi — view entire organic recipe.
management.chemical_summary: Systemic fungicides target active root pathogens — check exact doses.

Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like maize or sorghum for 2-3 seasons.
chemical_practices: Dress seeds with Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP at the rate of 2g/kg seed.
Drench the infected plant patches and surrounding soil with Carbendazim 50% WP or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC.

disease_info.cause: The fungal pathogen Aspergillus niger attacks seeds, seedlings, and hypocotyls. The fungus thrives in warm temperatures (30-35°C), high soil moisture, and high soil humidity. Seed injury or physical damage during planting provides entry points for the pathogen.
disease_info.symptoms: The hypocotyl region becomes water-soaked, turns black, and decays. Rapid wilting of seedlings occurs, and the affected collar region of the stem is covered with a black mass of fungal spores.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soilborne fungus thrives in warm soils — upgrade to unlock more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through infected seeds and soilborne fungal spores. Wind, irrigation water, and farming tools also assist in carrying the spores from one plant to another.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Dark decaying lesions near soil line — see full diagnostic details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores travel via soil, water, and seeds — get details.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Groundnut roots have a fungal disease. You can see a dark rot spreading across the collar region and roots of the seedling. The fungus is called Aspergillus niger. It spreads through contaminated soil, infected seeds, and high soil moisture.

disease_info.cause: Basal Stem Rot is caused by the soil-borne wood-decaying fungus Ganoderma. It primarily attacks older palms, entering through roots damaged by poor drainage, high soil moisture, waterlogging, or mechanical injury.

disease_info.cause: The larva of the Leucinodes orbonalis moth bores into the tender shoots of the eggplant during its vegetative stage. It feeds on internal tissues, blocking the vascular system of the plant, which results in the wilting and eventual death of the growing tips.
disease_info.symptoms: Visible symptoms include the wilting and drooping of tender apical shoots, presence of frass or insect excrement at the entry hole on the stem, and subsequent drying of the affected branch.
disease_info.cause_summary: Borer pest bores into stems disrupting sap flow - learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The adult female moth lays eggs on the undersides of leaves, tender shoots, and flower buds. Upon hatching, the larvae immediately bore into the plant tissue, meaning the spread is driven by the moth's flight and egg-laying activity.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Drooping wilted shoots with boreholes and frass - details inside.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Moths fly to lay eggs on tender tissues - upgrade now.

analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Immediately clip and destroy all wilted shoots. Install pheromone traps to disrupt the moth mating cycle, and apply systemic insecticides such as Chlorantraniliprole to protect new vegetative growth from larval boring.

disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen thrives in humidity, spreading fast — upgrade to learn more.

disease_info.cause: Caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), which invades the plant through the roots, colonizes the vascular system (xylem), and blocks water and nutrient transport, leading to wilting and eventual death of the plant.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms include yellowing and wilting of older leaves, typically starting from the margins and progressing inwards. The base of the pseudostem often shows dark brown to black discoloration, and internal vascular tissues exhibit reddish-brown streaks when cut.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil-borne fungus invades roots, blocks water flow, causing wilt. Upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Fusarium Wilt spreads primarily through infected soil adhering to farm tools, machinery, and footwear. It can also spread through contaminated irrigation water and, critically, through infected suckers used as planting material.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Older leaves yellow, wilt; pseudostem base darkens. See full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Soil-borne pathogen spreads via tools, water, and infected suckers. Unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Immediately remove infected plants
steps.description: Carefully uproot and destroy all plants showing clear signs of Fusarium Wilt. Ensure no plant debris remains in the field as it can harbor the fungus and facilitate spread.

steps.label: Day 2 — Morning
steps.title: Sanitize all farm tools
steps.description: Thoroughly clean and disinfect all farming tools, equipment, and footwear used in the affected area. Use a 10% bleach solution or an equivalent agricultural disinfectant to prevent pathogen transfer.

steps.label: Day 3 — Afternoon
steps.title: Apply beneficial soil microbes
steps.description: Drench the soil around healthy surrounding banana plants with a commercial formulation of Trichoderma viride. This can help enhance soil health and suppress the activity of the Fusarium fungus.

steps.label: Day 5 — Morning
steps.title: Improve field drainage
steps.description: Ensure proper drainage in the field to avoid waterlogging, which often favors the growth and spread of fungal pathogens. Consider creating shallow trenches to divert excess water.

steps.label: Day 7 — Inspection
steps.title: Monitor surrounding plants
steps.description: Regularly and closely inspect nearby banana plants for any new or developing symptoms such as leaf yellowing, wilting, or pseudostem discoloration. Early detection is crucial.

steps.label: Day 10 — Planning
steps.title: Avoid replanting bananas
steps.description: Do not replant banana in the currently infected soil for a period of several years. Explore crop rotation with non-host plants like paddy or sugarcane to break the disease cycle.

steps.label: Day 14 — Future Steps
steps.title: Source resistant varieties
steps.description: For all future plantings, commit to using only tissue-cultured, disease-free planting material of Fusarium wilt-resistant banana varieties to establish a healthy and sustainable farm.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora parasitica var. piperina. It is highly active under conditions of high soil moisture, waterlogging, prolonged rainfall, and elevated relative humidity. Warm temperatures with poor drainage create the ideal environment for the spores to germinate and infect the root and lower leaf tissues.
disease_info.symptoms: Visible symptoms include water-soaked, dark brown or black lesions starting from the leaf tips or margins. These lesions expand rapidly, turning the leaf tissue soft, rot-like, and eventually causing it to dry up and fall off. Leaf chlorosis followed by severe wilting of the vine is also common as the infection progresses.

disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through soil-borne zoospores that swim in water films. It is also transmitted through infected planting material, splashing rain or irrigation water, and contaminated agricultural tools used during pruning or vine tying.

disease_info.disease_spread: Spores are spread by splashing water, wind-driven rain, contaminated tools, machinery, and workers moving through wet foliage. Seed-borne transmission is also a major spread mechanism.
