organic_practices: Sanitation: Regularly remove and destroy severely infected leaves by pruning them from the plant and burying or burning the debris away from the plantation. This reduces the fungal inoculum.
Improve Air Circulation: Maintain proper plant spacing and judiciously prune older, non-productive leaves to enhance air movement within the canopy, reducing humidity and leaf wetness.
Balanced Nutrition: Ensure plants receive adequate and balanced fertilization, especially potassium, to improve overall plant vigor and natural resistance to diseases.
Mulching: Apply organic mulch around the plant base to help retain soil moisture, suppress weeds, and reduce soil splash of spores onto lower leaves.

Biological Agents: Consider foliar applications or soil drenching with microbial antagonists like Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis, which can promote plant health and offer some disease suppression.
chemical_practices: Systemic Fungicides: Azoxystrobin, Difenoconazole, Propiconazole, Epoxiconazole. These are absorbed by the plant and provide protection from within.
Contact Fungicides: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil. These provide a protective barrier on the leaf surface and are often used in rotation or mixture with systemic fungicides.
Rotation: Implement a strict fungicide rotation program using different active ingredients and modes of action to prevent the development of fungicide resistance in the pathogen.

disease_info.cause: Black Sigatoka is caused by the fungus Pseudocercospora fijiensis. The disease thrives in warm, humid conditions with extended periods of leaf wetness. Spores are primarily dispersed by wind and rain, landing on healthy banana leaves where they germinate and penetrate the leaf tissue, leading to infection.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms are small, reddish-brown streaks on the lower leaf surface, typically appearing on the third or fourth youngest leaves. These streaks enlarge, become elongated, and turn dark brown to black, often surrounded by a prominent yellow halo. As the disease progresses, lesions merge, leading to extensive necrosis, chlorosis (yellowing), and premature death of entire leaf sections. Severely infected leaves shrivel and appear burnt.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungus thrives in warm, humid conditions, causing severe leaf damage. Upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads through airborne conidia (asexual spores) and ascospores (sexual spores) carried by wind and rain splash. Infected plant debris on the ground also serves as a source of inoculum. High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness are crucial for spore germination and infection, allowing rapid dissemination within a plantation.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Elongated dark spots with yellow halos, merging to cause necrosis. See full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spreads rapidly via wind, rain, and infected plant debris. Unlock complete guide.

steps.label: Day 10 — Afternoon

steps.label: Day 14 — Afternoon

steps.description: Thoroughly inspect all plants. If disease is still active, plan another fungicide application with a different active ingredient. Continue sanitation and monitoring weekly to prevent recurrence.

disease_info.disease_spread: Spores are highly light and easily dispersed by wind currents, rain splash, and mechanical farm tools. The disease is also spread extensively through infected seed setts used during planting.

Affected sheaths may fail to exert the panicle completely, causing it to rot inside or emerge with discolored, chaffy, and sterile grains. A powdery white-to-pinkish fungal growth can sometimes be seen inside the affected sheaths.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV), which is classified in the Begomovirus genus of the family Geminiviridae. It is primarily transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) in a persistent, circulative manner. Once the virus enters the plant vascular system, it disrupts physiological processes, resulting in chlorosis, severe leaf curling, and stunted development.
disease_info.symptoms: Prominent symptoms include severe upward curling and cupping of the leaf margins, yellowing (interveinal chlorosis) of the foliage, especially on young leaves, reduced leaf size, and overall stunting of the plant. Flowers may drop prematurely, leading to a drastic reduction in fruit set.
disease_info.cause_summary: Viral pathogen transmitted by whiteflies harms crops; upgrade for details.
disease_info.disease_spread: The virus is not transmitted mechanically or through seeds. It is spread solely by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci) as it feeds on the phloem of infected plants and subsequently migrates to healthy hosts. Wind currents can carry these small insects over significant distances, accelerating local epidemics.

disease_info.cause: Powdery Mildew is caused by the fungus Podosphaera xanthii (formerly known as Sphaerotheca fuliginea). It thrives in warm, dry day climates followed by humid nights. High relative humidity promotes spore germination, while dry conditions allow the spores to spread easily via wind. Unlike most other fungi, free water on the leaf surface can actually inhibit its growth, but high ambient humidity is highly favorable.
disease_info.symptoms: The most prominent symptom is the appearance of white, talcum powder-like spots or patches on the upper and lower surfaces of the leaves, petioles, and young stems. As the infection progresses, these patches expand to cover entire leaves, causing them to turn yellow, dry up, brown, and eventually drop prematurely, leaving the fruit exposed to sunscald.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogen thrives in humidity, spreading fast — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The fungal spores (conidia) are primary spreaders and are carried by wind currents over long distances to healthy plants. It can also overwinter in plant debris, weeds, or alternate hosts, serving as a source of primary inoculum for the next crop cycle.

disease_info.disease_spread: The virus is not sap-transmissible or seed-borne. It is spread primarily by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci) from infected papaya plants or alternative weed hosts to healthy crops.

As the disease progresses, these sticky drops dry up and are replaced by dark brown to black sclerotia (hard fungal structures) which project out from the glumes in place of normal grain.

disease_info.disease_spread: Initial infection originates from soil-borne sclerotia left over from previous crop residues, or seed contamination. disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the soil-borne fungus Rhizoctonia solani. This pathogen thrives in cool, excessively wet soils and poorly drained fields. Over-watering, combined with heavy, compacted clay soils, deprives roots of oxygen and allows the fungus to aggressively attack vulnerable seedling tissues near the soil line.
disease_info.symptoms: The primary symptom is the collapse and wilting of the young bean seedling. The stem near the soil line shows dark brown, water-soaked, sunken lesions. The leaves are drooping, dry, and shriveling, indicating that the damaged stem can no longer transport water and nutrients upward from the root system.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil fungal pathogen thrives in waterlogged conditions — upgrade to unlock.
disease_info.disease_spread: Rhizoctonia solani is primarily a soil-borne fungus that survives in soil organic matter or as sclerotia. It spreads across the field through splashing water from rain or overhead irrigation, movement of contaminated soil on farm machinery, tools, shoes, and infected plant residues left in the field.

disease_info.cause: The premature shedding of cotton squares, flowers, and young bolls is primarily triggered by environmental and physiological stress. Major causes include severe soil moisture fluctuations (drought followed by heavy rain or waterlogging), high temperature stress during the reproductive phase, insufficient light due to prolonged cloudy weather, and nutrient imbalances (especially nitrogen or boron deficiencies). Under stress, the plant produces excessive ethylene or abscisic acid, leading to the formation of an abscission layer at the base of the stalk, causing the structures to drop.
disease_info.symptoms: The main symptom is the presence of fallen squares, young bolls, and dried flower buds on the ground beneath the cotton plants. The abscised parts may appear healthy or slightly withered with a clean break at the point of detachment. The remaining canopy might show signs of water stress (wilting), nitrogen deficiency (yellowing leaves), or excessive vegetative growth at the expense of reproductive structures.
disease_info.cause_summary: Physiological stress triggers premature shedding - unlock premium tips for stability.
disease_info.disease_spread: This is a physiological disorder and is not caused by an infectious pathogen. Therefore, it does not spread from plant to plant like fungal, bacterial, or viral diseases. However, the entire field can show similar symptoms simultaneously because all plants are exposed to the same adverse environmental stresses or soil management conditions.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Fallen squares and young bolls on ground - get full report.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Non-infectious physiological stress conditions spread fieldwide - explore corrective measures.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the soil-borne fungus Sclerotium oryzae. It thrives in conditions of high nitrogen fertilization, stagnant standing water, and close planting which creates a humid microclimate around the tillers. The fungus overwinters as sclerotia in crop residues and soil, which float on water and infect the rice sheaths at the water line.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms appear as dark, water-soaked, irregular lesions on the outer leaf sheaths near the water line. As the disease progresses, the fungus penetrates inward, causing the inner sheaths and stem (culm) to rot. The stem weakens, leading to lodging, while numerous tiny, black, mustard-seed-like sclerotia develop inside the hollow stem. Infected tillers produce partially filled or empty panicles.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil fungal pathogen thrives in standing water—upgrade for details.
disease_info.disease_spread: The primary survival and dispersal structures are sclerotia, which persist in the soil and crop debris. When fields are flooded, these sclerotia float to the water surface, accumulate around the rice tillers, and initiate infection. The disease spreads within the field via irrigation water carrying the floating sclerotia and during harvesting when infected straw is moved.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Dark rotting stems and lodging detected—upgrade to view guide.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Waterborne floating sclerotia spread infection—upgrade to prevent transmission.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the Papaya leaf curl virus, which is a Geminivirus. It is primarily transmitted from infected plants to healthy ones by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci). The virus cannot infect plants mechanically through simple contact but relies heavily on the insect vector population dynamics.
disease_info.symptoms: Severe downward curling, crinkling, and distortion of the leaves. The affected leaves become leathery, brittle, and significantly reduced in size. The petioles show twisting, and infected plants exhibit stunted growth with reduced fruit yield and quality.
disease_info.cause_summary: Viral pathogen transmitted by whiteflies — upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: The virus is spread primarily by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) vector. It can also be transmitted through infected grafting material or infected seedlings. It is not transmitted through seed, soil, or direct physical contact between plants.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Severe leaf curling and distortion detected — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Whiteflies transmit the virus rapidly — upgrade for spread vectors.

disease_info.cause: Caused primarily by nutrient deficiencies of phosphorus and zinc in the soil. High soil acidity (low pH) or cold temperatures can lock up these nutrients, rendering them unavailable to the guava root system.
disease_info.symptoms: Leaves turn a distinct bronze, purplish, or reddish color starting from the margins and progressing inward. Growth of the branches is stunted, and affected leaves may eventually drop prematurely.
disease_info.cause_summary: Nutrient deficiency triggered by soil acidity - unlock our nutrient handbook.
disease_info.disease_spread: This is a physiological nutritional disorder and is not infectious. It does not spread from plant to plant via pathogens but can affect whole orchards simultaneously if they share the same soil conditions.

disease_info.symptoms: Upward curling of leaves, crinkling, puckering, reduced leaf size, short internodes, and stunted plant growth. Leaf veins may also appear thickened, and infected plants produce fewer or no flowers and fruits.

disease_info.disease_spread: The virus is not mechanically transmitted or seed-borne. It spreads entirely through the feeding activity of infected whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) from diseased crops or alternative weed hosts to healthy plants.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Upward curling puckering leaves and stunted crop plant growth — upgrade.

organic_practices: Crop Rotation: Rotate brinjal with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2-3 years to break the disease cycle and reduce inoculum in the soil, preventing pathogen build-up.
Sanitation: Remove and destroy all infected plant debris from the field immediately after harvest. Prune and dispose of severely infected leaves during the growing season to minimize spore sources.
Proper Spacing: Ensure adequate plant spacing to improve air circulation within the canopy, which helps reduce leaf wetness and humidity, unfavorable for fungal growth.
Water Management: Avoid overhead irrigation, especially in the evening, to minimize prolonged leaf wetness. Use drip irrigation if possible to keep foliage dry.

Neem Oil/Bio-fungicides: For early stages or as a preventive, apply neem oil (a natural repellent/fungicide) or bio-fungicides containing beneficial microbes like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma viride.
chemical_practices: Chlorothalonil: Apply a foliar spray of Chlorothalonil, a broad-spectrum protectant fungicide, according to label rates, especially during periods favorable for disease development.
Mancozeb: Use Mancozeb, another protective fungicide, starting applications early in the season and repeating as necessary to form a protective barrier on leaves.

Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole: Systemic fungicides like a combination of Azoxystrobin (strobilurin) and Difenoconazole (triazole) can provide both curative and protective action against the disease, offering broader control.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the fungus Ramulariopsis atrolaetevirens (formerly known as Ramularia areola). It thrives in environments with high relative humidity (above 85%), frequent rainfall, and moderate temperatures ranging between 20°C and 30°C. Overcrowded plant spacing, which restricts airflow and traps moisture within the crop canopy, significantly accelerates the infection process.
disease_info.symptoms: The leaf shows characteristic whitish to pale grey, powdery, angular mildew patches restricted by the leaf veins on the upper surface. This corresponds to a dense growth of fungal conidiophores and conidia primarily on the lower surface, giving the spots an 'areolate' or block-like appearance. As the infection progresses, the affected leaf tissue becomes chlorotic, then necrotic, leading to premature leaf fall starting from the lower canopy.

disease_info.disease_spread: The fungus survives in crop debris from previous seasons as dormant mycelium or chlamydospores. Primary infection occurs when wind currents and splashing rain carry spores (conidia) from the soil or debris to the lower leaves of healthy plants. Secondary spread occurs rapidly through wind and rain splash within the field during warm, humid conditions.

analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Prune infected leaves immediately, switch from overhead irrigation to drip, and apply copper hydroxide sprays every 7-10 days under warm, wet conditions.

disease_info.cause: The primary cause is Pythium fungal pathogens, which thrive in excessively wet, cool-to-warm soils. Poor soil drainage, overwatering, and proximity to cold drip lines can trigger this infection in young seedlings, damaging the stem base and cotyledons.
disease_info.symptoms: The cotyledons show water-soaked lesions, marginal yellowing, and slight curling or distortion. The seedling stem near the soil line is restricted, weakened, and may collapse entirely.
disease_info.cause_summary: Fungal pathogens thrive in wet, poorly drained soil conditions — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread: Pythium spreads through soil-borne water, splashing rain, or irrigation water moving across infected soil. It rapidly moves from seedling to seedling under damp conditions through shared root zones.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Water-soaked lesions on cotyledons with stem constriction — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Pathogens spread via wet soil and splashing irrigation water — upgrade.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Cucumber has a early seedling fungal infection. You can see water-soaked spots, browning, and slight distortion on the young cotyledon leaves. The soil-borne fungus is called Pythium. It spreads through wet soil, high moisture, and dripping water around young roots.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Reduce irrigation immediately to let soil dry, and drench the root zone with Trichoderma-based bio-fungicide or metalaxyl-M to protect young root tissue.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the soil-borne fungal pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. medicaginis. It infects the plant through the root system, colonizing and blocking the water-conducting xylem vessels, leading to progressive wilting, stunting, and eventual death of the plant.
disease_info.symptoms: Visible symptoms include a distinctive reddish-brown to dark brown discoloration of the vascular tissue inside the split taproot and stem. Leaves turn pale, wilt, and curl downwards, often starting on one side of the plant before the entire stem dies.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil fungal pathogen restricts xylem water flow — upgrade to learn.
disease_info.disease_spread: The fungus survives as spores in the soil for several years and spreads through infected plant debris, movement of contaminated soil, farm machinery, irrigation water, and infected seeds.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Dark brown vascular discoloration inside taproot visible — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores survive in soil, spreading via machinery — unlock details.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the fungus Cercospora sojina, which survives in infected crop residue and seeds. The pathogen thrives under warm, humid conditions (25°C to 30°C) accompanied by frequent rainfall or heavy dew, leading to rapid spore germination and penetration of the leaf tissue.

disease_info.symptoms_summary: Grey-tan lesions with dark reddish-brown borders and chlorotic halos.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Spores spread through wind and rain splashes during warm weather.

disease_info.cause: Burr knots are clusters of primordial roots that develop on the above-ground trunk or branches of apple trees. They are primarily a physiological disorder caused by genetic susceptibility (highly common in certain rootstocks like M.7, M.9, and MM.111), high humidity, shaded conditions, and the presence of organic debris around the trunk base.
disease_info.symptoms: Visible rough, swollen, gall-like growths on the trunk. Numerous small, pinkish-to-brownish root initials or finger-like root protrusions erupt from these swellings, typically on shaded portions of the lower trunk.

disease_info.disease_spread: This is a physiological condition, not an infectious disease, so it does not spread from tree to tree. However, it can expand on the same tree, especially under damp, shaded conditions, and can serve as an entry point for pests like dogwood borer and woolly apple aphid, or pathogens like fire blight.

disease_info.cause: Panama disease, also known as Fusarium wilt of banana, is caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc). The fungus enters the plant through the roots and then colonizes the xylem vessels, which are responsible for water and nutrient transport. This colonization blocks the vascular system, leading to wilting and eventual death of the plant.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms include yellowing of older leaves, progressing from the margins inwards. The leaves eventually turn brown, wilt, and collapse, often remaining attached to the pseudostem. Splitting of the pseudostem base and reddish-brown discoloration of the vascular tissue inside the pseudostem are also characteristic signs upon cutting.
disease_info.cause_summary: Soil-borne fungal pathogen invades roots, blocking water flow—unlock insights.
disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through infected soil, water (especially irrigation water), contaminated farm tools and machinery, and infected planting materials such as suckers or rhizomes. It does not spread through airborne spores affecting leaves, but rather through the movement of the fungus in soil or plant material.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Yellowing, browning, and wilting of older leaves evident—discover hidden signs.

organic_practices: Rake and destroy or deeply bury all fallen walnut leaves and debris around the tree base to eliminate overwintering fungal inoculum.
Prune lower canopy branches to improve air circulation and accelerate foliage drying after rain events.
Apply copper octanoate or liquid copper formulations during early spring leaf-out as a preventative measure.
chemical_practices: Apply preventative fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or tebuconazole starting at bud break.
Repeat chemical applications at 10 to 14-day intervals during wet spring periods, adhering strictly to pre-harvest intervals.
management.consumption_safety: Safe

market_quality.reasoning: While the foliage is showing mid-stage anthracnose infection which impacts photosynthetic efficiency and overall tree vigor, the nuts themselves may still be marketable if protected from husk infection. However, systemic orchard pressure lowers overall grade designation.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Sanitation and Canopy Inspection
steps.description: Prune away highly symptomatic leaves and collect any fallen leaves from the soil surface below the tree canopy to reduce immediate spore load.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Preventative Fungicide Application
steps.description: Spray the canopy with an approved copper-based fungicide or systemic fungicide like tebuconazole, ensuring thorough coverage of both upper and lower leaf surfaces.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Watering Management Adjustment
steps.description: Ensure irrigation is directed at the root zone only. Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that wets the foliage and facilitates fungal spore dispersal.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Evaluate Treatment Efficacy
steps.description: Inspect newly emerged walnut leaves for any fresh black spots. If wet weather persists and new symptoms appear, plan a follow-up fungicide rotation.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Walnut leaf has a fungal infection. You can see small, dark brown circular spots spreading across the leaf surface and margins. The fungus is called Ophiognomonia leptostyla. It spreads through wind and rain-splashes during warm, wet spring weather.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Sanitize fallen leaf debris immediately and apply protective copper or systemic fungicides to prevent canopy spread during damp periods.

disease_info.cause: Small sucking pests, mainly aphids and jassids, harbor on the underside of cotton leaves. They thrive in dry weather conditions with occasional rains, drawing sap from the leaves and causing physical damage and physiological stress to the plant.
disease_info.symptoms: Underside of the leaf shows tiny crawling green insects along the main veins. Early symptoms include leaf curling, yellowing of margins, and a slight shiny, sticky appearance due to honeydew excretion.
disease_info.cause_summary: Sucking pests thrive under dry weather - unlock full pest profile.
disease_info.disease_spread: Winged adults fly from nearby infested fields, weeds, or alternate hosts. They multiply rapidly under warm, humid conditions and are carried across the farm by wind currents.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Leaf curling and tiny green insects - view complete symptoms guide.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Pests spread by wind and flight - unlock dispersal patterns.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Monitor and Install Sticky Traps
steps.description: Inspect the undersides of leaves throughout the field. Install bright yellow sticky traps slightly above the crop canopy to capture winged adults.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Botanical Spray
steps.description: Spray the crop thoroughly with neem oil mixed with a few drops of liquid soap. Ensure the spray covers the undersides of the leaves where the insects hide.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Re-evaluate Pest Population
steps.description: Check the leaf undersides again to see if insect counts have dropped. If populations are still high or spreading, prepare for a targeted chemical application.

steps.label: Day 10
steps.title: Apply Target Insecticide
steps.description: If pest count exceeds the economic threshold (more than 5-10 pests per leaf), apply a systemic insecticide such as Acetamiprid.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Cotton leaves have a sucking pest infestation. You can see small, light-green insects crawling on the veins of the lower leaf surface. The primary pests are called Cotton Aphids and Jassids. They spread easily to neighboring plants through wind and short-distance flight.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Install yellow sticky traps immediately and spray neem oil (1500 ppm) at 5 ml/L of water, ensuring thorough coverage under the leaves. If pest pressure remains high after a week, apply a systemic chemical like Acetamiprid 20% SP to prevent severe leaf curling.

management.chemical_summary: Effective insecticides target larval stages—upgrade for dosage details.

Release Trichogramma chilonis egg parasitoids at 50,000 per acre.

chemical_practices: Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC
Flubendiamide 39.35% SC
Indoxacarb 14.5% SC

disease_info.cause: Feeding activity of caterpillars and beetles, specifically Spodoptera litura (Tobacco cutworm) and other defoliating insects that chew holes through the leaf tissue, leaving characteristic skeletonized patterns.
disease_info.symptoms: Irregularly shaped holes in the leaves, skeletonization where only the veins remain, and chewed edges on the foliage.
disease_info.cause_summary: Feeding caterpillars chew holes in leaves—upgrade to learn more.
disease_info.disease_spread: Caterpillars crawl locally between touching foliage, while adult moths fly long distances to lay eggs on the undersides of leaves.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Chewed leaves with irregular holes detected—see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Moths fly and lay eggs on leaves—upgrade for insights.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Manual Larvae Removal and Scouting
steps.description: Handpick and destroy visible caterpillars on the leaves to immediately reduce the pest population in small-scale areas.

steps.label: Day 3 — Evening
steps.title: Apply Biological Spray Treatment
steps.description: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or Neem-based formulation thoroughly on both sides of the leaves where caterpillars feed.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Monitor Defoliation Levels
steps.description: Assess the field to see if fresh feeding holes are appearing or if the pest population has successfully decreased.

steps.label: Day 10
steps.title: Follow-up Target Insecticide Application
steps.description: If defoliation continues to exceed economic thresholds, apply a targeted chemical insecticide containing Chlorantraniliprole.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your Soybean leaves have a pest defoliation problem. You can see irregular holes and missing leaf tissue where feeding occurred. The caterpillar pest responsible is called Spodoptera litura. It spreads when adult moths fly to healthy plants to deposit their eggs.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Manually collect larvae, set pheromone traps, and apply Bt or Chlorantraniliprole to control the defoliators.

management.organic_summary: Use yellow traps and botanical sprays to control vectors — upgrade.
management.chemical_summary: Systemic insecticides successfully suppress vector populations — see dosage.
organic_practices: Install yellow sticky traps at a rate of 10-15 traps per acre to capture adult whiteflies.
Spray neem oil (10,000 ppm) at 3 ml per liter of water to deter feeding and egg-laying by vectors.
Remove and destroy severely infected plants and weed hosts immediately to reduce the source of virus inoculum.
chemical_practices: Spray systemic insecticides such as Imidacloprid (17.8% SL) at 0.5 ml per liter of water to manage whiteflies.
Apply Acetamiprid (20% SP) at 0.4 grams per liter of water as an alternative rotation to prevent insecticide resistance.

disease_info.cause: The disease is caused by the Chilli leaf curl virus (ChiLCV), which is a geminivirus. It is transmitted in a persistent, circulative manner by the silverleaf whitefly vector.
disease_info.symptoms: Leaves exhibit upward curling of the margins, puckering, crinkling, and reduction in size. The plant shows stunted growth with shortened internodes and a bushy appearance.
disease_info.cause_summary: Viral pathogen transmitted by whiteflies causes severe leaf puckering — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread: The virus is spread primarily by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci). It is not transmitted mechanically through touch, nor is it seed-borne, but it can persist in weeds surrounding the field.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Upward curling and stunting of leaves is visible — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Whiteflies transmit the virus across fields quickly — unlock premium.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Remove Affected Plants and Install Traps
steps.description: Carefully uproot and burn the severely stunted plants showing extreme leaf curling to eliminate the source of virus. Immediately install 15 yellow sticky traps per acre near the plant canopy to monitor and capture whiteflies.

steps.label: Day 2 — Morning
steps.title: Apply First Vector Control Spray
steps.description: Spray Imidacloprid (17.8% SL) at 0.5 ml per liter of water during the early morning hours, ensuring thorough coverage on the undersides of the leaves where whiteflies live.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Nutritional Support and Field Sanitation
steps.description: Apply a balanced foliar fertilizer containing micronutrients to boost the immunity of recovering plants. Keep the field free of wild weed hosts.

steps.label: Day 10
steps.title: Apply Rotational Insecticide Spray
steps.description: Spray Acetamiprid (20% SP) at 0.4 grams per liter of water to target newly hatched whitefly nymphs and prevent them from spreading the virus further.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Evaluate Vector and Leaf Symptoms
steps.description: Check the sticky traps and the undersides of new leaves for any remaining whiteflies. Ensure new leaf growth appears flat and healthy.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your ದೊಣ್ಣೆ ಮೆಣಸಿನಕಾಯಿ (ಕ್ಯಾಪ್ಸಿಕಂ) leaves have a viral infection causing distortion. You can see the leaves curling upwards and the overall plant growth looks stunted. The virus is called Chilli Leaf Curl Virus. It spreads through tiny whitefly insects that carry the pathogen from infected weeds to healthy crops.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Uproot infected plants immediately, set up yellow sticky traps, and spray systemic insecticides like Imidacloprid to control the whitefly vector spreading the virus.

management.organic_summary: Sticky traps and neem oil sprays suppress pest populations — unlock complete guide.
management.chemical_summary: Systemic insecticides provide rapid knockdown of sucking pests — upgrade for dosage guide.
organic_practices: Install blue sticky traps at canopy level to monitor and capture adult thrips.
Spray 1% Neem Oil solution or Azadirachtin (1500 ppm) at 3-5 ml per liter of water during early morning or late evening.
Release natural predators like predatory mites (Amblyseius spp.) or pirate bugs (Orius spp.) to biologically control populations.
chemical_practices: Spray Fipronil 5% SC at 2 ml per liter of water to quickly reduce thrips pressure.
Apply Spinetoram 11.7% SC at 0.8 ml per liter of water for targeted systemic control.
Alternate chemical classes to prevent the rapid development of pesticide resistance.
management.consumption_safety: As this is a growing plant with leaf damage, the future fruit remains safe for consumption, provided pesticide withdrawal periods are strictly followed before harvesting.

disease_info.cause: Infestation by microscopic thrips feeding on tender young foliage, sucking sap and causing physical deformation.
disease_info.symptoms: Leaves showing upward curling, puckering, crinkling, and characteristic silvery or bronzed scarred patches on the margins and undersides.
disease_info.cause_summary: Sucking pests attack tender foliage in warm weather — upgrade.
disease_info.disease_spread: Thrips fly short distances and are carried rapidly by wind currents, moving quickly from plant to plant.
disease_info.symptoms_summary: Upward curling and puckered leaves with bronzed margins — see full details.
disease_info.disease_spread_summary: Wind and active flying rapidly spread pests across fields — upgrade.

steps.label: Day 1 (Today)
steps.title: Install Traps and Prune Damaged Tips
steps.description: Hang blue sticky traps 15 cm above the plant canopy to trap adult thrips. Carefully prune and safely dispose of heavily deformed, severely damaged leaf tips.

steps.label: Day 3 — Morning
steps.title: Apply Targeted Insecticide Spray
steps.description: Spray Spinetoram 11.7% SC at 0.8 ml/liter of water. Direct the spray thoroughly to the undersides of leaves where thrips actively hide and feed.

steps.label: Day 7
steps.title: Assess Population and Trap Catch
steps.description: Examine new growing tips for signs of puckering. Check sticky traps to determine if the population of flying adult thrips has decreased significantly.

steps.label: Day 10
steps.title: Follow up with Neem Oil
steps.description: Apply a preventive spray of cold-pressed Neem Oil (1500 ppm) at 5 ml/liter of water with a organic emulsifier to target emerging nymphs and break the life cycle.

steps.label: Day 14
steps.title: Nutrient Support and Final Review
steps.description: Apply a foliar spray of micronutrients and soluble nitrogen to stimulate fresh, healthy vegetative flush and help the plant recover from feeding stress.

analysis_raw_en.What_is_happening: Your ದೊಣ್ಣೆ ಮೆಣಸಿನಕಾಯಿ (ಕ್ಯಾಪ್ಸಿಕಂ) has a sucking pest infestation. You can see leaves curling upward, puckering, and developing dark or scarred margins. The tiny insect responsible is called Thrips. It spreads rapidly through wind currents and quickly moves to fresh, healthy foliage.
analysis_raw_en.quick_treatment_summary: Prune severely distorted tips, install blue sticky traps, and spray Spinetoram or Neem Oil targeting leaf undersides to halt thrips feeding.
